item.description:
Mahmoud Elsherif; wanyin li; Meyrem Tompson; Kevin Paterson · PsyArXiv

The Age of Acquisition (AoA) effect is where words acquired during childhood are recognised more quickly than those acquired during adulthood. However, the influence of AoA on compound words and its stability across the adult lifespan remain under-investigated. We conducted two eye-tracking experiments to clarify how the AoA effect is moderated by ageing and spacing. Ninety British English adults participated across two eye-tracking experiments: 60 young adults (30 reading unspaced compounds in Experiment 1 and 30 reading spaced compounds in Experiment 2) and 30 older adults (who read both unspaced and spaced compounds across experiments). The Macarthur-Bates Communicative Development Inventories (CDI) are a set of widely used parent-report instruments for measuring young children’s language development. The most widely used measures for English-speaking children are the CDIs for 8-30 months. There is a strong need for both clinical and research purpose for comparable measures for three-year-olds. The previously published U.S. English CDI-III yielded norms for 30-37 months only, due to ceiling effects, and assessed limited aspects of language. item.description:
Sarah Akkad; Ashley Wong Ke Wei; Mary-Claire Ball; Sharon Wolf; Kaja K. Jasińska · PsyArXiv

Internally-displaced children often lack schooling and reside in highly multilingual contexts. In Nigeria, children must learn to read in a local language (e.g., Hausa), and English; here, language skills can transfer across languages to support biliteracy. Importantly, the strength of transfer is constrained by proficiency in language skills. Formal schooling and early life exposure are crucial for acquisition of language skills. Nez Perce is a language with a dedicated comparative morpheme and crisp judgments in its comparatives, but with no means to express differential measurement in its comparative. These data can be captured by two different types of analyses: either Nez Perce has a negative setting of the Degree Semantics Parameter ([±DSP]) (Beck et al., 2009), along with a comparative operator that allows manipulation of context (Klein, 1980), or it has a positive setting of said parameter, but the comparative operator does not provide a slot for a differential degree argument. item.title: Third readings by semantic scope lowering: Prolepsis in Tiwa
item.dc:creator: Dawson, Virginia
Deal, Amy Rose
item.description:
Dawson, Virginia; Deal, Amy Rose · Zenodo

Tiwa (Tibeto-Burman; India) attitude reports allow for proleptic objects, base-generated in the matrix clause but semantically related to a bound pronoun in the embedded clause. Unlike prolepsis in German (Salzmann, 2017b) and Nez Perce (Deal, 2018), which only allow for classic de re readings of the proleptic object, Tiwa prolepsis supports both classic de re and third readings. We provide an analysis that derives third readings via semantic scope lowering, an analytical relative of semantic reconstruction, and consider cross-linguistic implications.

Reading is a fundamental life skill, and at its basis is the ability to process single words. Researchers often study single-word processing using lexical decision tasks. In addition, best-practice knowledge is often only transmitted informally within labs, leading to heterogeneity and reduced reproducibility across labs. Traditional methods of thematic analysis are critical for deep, nuanced understanding of complex planning challenges, but the manual intensity of the process limits its applications to increasingly large datasets generated by planning processes. Hybrid, supervised methods of natural language processing offer a solution by allowing researchers to scale theory-driven topics by using traditional methods to first label a sample of the data. Research on linguistic illusions has debated what information is used to access memory representations, but how speakers use surface phonological information during dependency resolution remains unclear. Agreement attraction is more likely when the attractor matches the form of an agreement controller (e.g., in case marking). This has been attributed to phonological forms directly activating every feature set they can express, regardless of context. Alternatively, form may act indirectly, by shifting the estimated probability that a noun is a controller, which retrieval uses as a cue. item.description:
Sihan Chen; Antonio Benítez-Burraco · PsyArXiv

The most distinctive feature of language is perhaps the ability to produce and comprehend utterances that have never been said before. This requires language to be transparent: comprehenders can infer the meaning of an utterance based on its components and the rules used to combine them. However, arbitrary associations between form and meaning (conventionality) are ubiquitous in language, despite them being difficult to learn. This is true for words, but also for many utterances. Why is this the case? In this paper, we propose languages balance conventionality and transparency by minimizing the communication and learning cost. Spontaneous speech is full of false starts, rephrasing, and speech errors. Speakers’ ability to detect errors and other problems in their own speech is commonly explained by monitoring mechanisms that rely on pre-articulatory representations, production states, or derivative predictions. We develop an alternative, cue-integrative account in which verbal self-monitoring is a natural consequence of what we have previously termed self-comprehension: speakers’ integration of contextual and sensory information to understand their own unfolding speech without requiring that meaning or intention be fully specified before articulation. item.description:
Alejandrina Cristia; Yasuyo MINAGAWA; Natalia Egorova-Brumley; Judit Gervain; Lucas Filippin; Dominique Cabrol; Emmanuel Dupoux · PsyArXiv

The present study investigated the neural correlates of infant discrimination of very similar linguistic varieties (Quebecois and Parisian French) using functional Near InfraRed Spectroscopy. In line with previous behavioral and electrophysiological data, there was no evidence that 3-month-olds discriminated the two regional accents, whereas 5-month-olds did, with the locus of discrimination in left anterior perisylvian regions. These neuroimaging results suggest that a developing language network relying crucially on left perisylvian cortices sustains infants’ discrimination of similar linguistic varieties within this early period of infancy.
